extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, patent practitioners, patent_office_staff, inventors, industry stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing legislative reforms in the America Invents Act (AIA) — e.g., first-inventor-to-file, post-grant review, prior user rights, supplemental examination — with respect to patent quality, certainty, constitutionality, and practical effects on inventors and industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve patent quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent reform should improve patent quality and reduce issuance of low-quality patents (especially business-method patents) that enable nuisance litigation and extortion by non-practicing entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 18 is described as a targeted mechanism to allow PTO experts to reexamine legally questionable business-method patents through a temporary pilot program; goal is to remove poor-quality patents that 'weaken the patent system' and 'cost companies and their customers millions of dollars.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce PTO backlog and modernize administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Reform should reduce the current PTO backlog and modernize agency procedures so the Office can process applications and new proceedings efficiently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislation must be judged on its ability to reduce the backlog and modernize the PTO; critics note the agency also needs resources and should be allowed to collect and allocate fee revenue rather than rely solely on appropriations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide greater certainty for patent rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative changes should increase certainty for inventors and patent holders about the scope, priority, and enforceability of patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First-inventor-to-file and a clearer definition of 'prior art' are argued to produce stronger, more certain patents and reduce expensive litigation over priority dates and private disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt first-inventor-to-file for clarity and international harmonization
rubrics_metrics.description: Move to a first-inventor-to-file system to create an official, simple, transparent, and fair rule for establishing priority dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First-to-file reduces litigation about inventorship/priority, prevents fraudulent backdating, aligns U.S. rules with international practice, and encourages prompt provisional filings to secure public priority dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior user / prior commercial use defense
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a prior commercial use (prior user) defense so entities that invented and used a technology commercially (especially in manufacturing) can continue to use it even if a later patent issues to someone else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The defense is required to protect firms that keep processes secret to preserve trade secrets; under the AIA it generally requires that the commercial use occurred in the United States, which is intended to incentivize domestic manufacturing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental examination safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Supplemental examination allows patent owners to submit additional material to the PTO post-issuance, but it must not become an unchecked 'get out of jail free' mechanism that permits correction of deceptive or post-filing-only information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics warn supplemental examination could permit submission of information not available at original filing and insulate inequitable conduct claims; recommended PTO limits include prohibiting reexamination based on material that didn't exist at original filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-grant review of business-method patents (targeted, expert-led)
rubrics_metrics.description: A post-grant review (transitional review program) should permit the PTO to review the validity of certain business-method patents via expert administrative proceedings as an inexpensive alternative to district-court litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 18 is framed as a temporary pilot targeting legally questionable business-method patents (particularly in financial services), drafted with USPTO input; proponents say it will allow experts to evaluate patents against the best prior art and reduce frivolous suits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrow construction of 'covered business method patent'
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of 'covered business method patent' should be narrowly construed to target patents unique to the financial services industry (i.e., patents only a financial services provider would use to furnish a financial product or service).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: electronic check scanning is an intended target; patents usable across industries should be excluded. Section 18 was described as intended to focus narrowly on non-technological financial-services patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technological invention exception to business-method review
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents for technological inventions (whose novelty turns on a technical innovation over prior art) should be excluded from the business-method post-grant review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exception does not exclude a patent merely because it 'recites technology.' Excluded examples include mechanical and manufacturing inventions (e.g., machines to count, sort, and authenticate currency) whose novelty is technical.

rubrics_metrics.name: High initiation standard for PTO review ('more likely than not' invalid)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before the PTO may initiate a post-grant review, it should determine that the patent is 'more likely than not' invalid — a high evidentiary threshold to protect legitimate patentees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supporters emphasize the 'more likely than not' standard in Section 18 as a safeguard ensuring the PTO cannot review patents without strong initial evidence of invalidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-availability standard for prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrict the definition of 'prior art' so that public uses and sales count only if they make the invention available to the public; secret or private uses/sales should not qualify as prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limiting prior art to 'public availability' reduces costly discovery/litigation to prove secret offers or private demonstrations, making prior art determinations cheaper and clearer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-grant review as an inexpensive substitute for litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Design post-grant administrative proceedings to be a cheaper, expert-driven alternative to district court litigation for resolving key patent validity issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proponents argue that post-grant review by PTO experts will address issues more efficiently, reduce litigation costs, and allow key questions to be resolved without expensive court discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect small inventors and clarify grace period effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Reform should protect small inventors' interests by preserving reasonable grace-period protections and ensuring first-to-file does not unduly disadvantage those who need time for market research and investor pitches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concerns include lack of clarity about the 'grace period' under first-to-file; small inventors need clear rules to avoid being pre-empted by others who learn of their ideas and file first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid special-industry earmarks; apply reforms uniformly
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislation should avoid creating special exceptions or 'earmarks' that treat one industry (e.g., financial services or banks) differently without clear justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opponents argue Section 18 is a separate rule for financial-services-related patents; critics ask why reforms shouldn't affect all patents and industries equally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional limits and separation-of-powers concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure reforms respect constitutional limits (Article III separation of powers) and do not allow administrative agency review to effectively overturn final judicial judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some members cite Plaut and warn that routing final adjudications back to an administrative agency raises separation-of-powers issues; legislation should be carefully drafted to avoid constitutional infirmities.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO resource and fee management
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementation of new proceedings requires that the PTO have stable resources and authority to collect and allocate fees to administer new processes effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics note that without fee retention the PTO may lack resources to handle post-grant reviews, supplemental examinations, and other new mechanisms; Congress should permit PTO fee collection and allocation for effective implementation.
